body:
Gujarat did not have a single political administration

During the 19th century, the territory that forms present-day Gujarat was divided between areas directly administered by the British and numerous princely states ruled by Indian rulers under British paramountcy. This distinction is essential for understanding the reforms introduced in Baroda.

Important cities such as Ahmedabad, Surat and Bharuch were administered within the British-controlled Bombay Presidency. Baroda, Bhavnagar, Gondal, Junagadh and Nawanagar were among the princely states of the region. Their rulers retained varying degrees of control over internal administration, although the British exercised superior political authority.

Princely state

A princely state was an Indian-ruled territory that retained an internal government but acknowledged British paramountcy. It was not ordinarily administered as a British district, nor was it fully sovereign or independent of British control.

Direct administration and indirect rule

In British-administered districts, officials appointed through the colonial administration exercised governmental authority. District Collectors and other officers implemented revenue policies, maintained public order and carried out administrative instructions under the Bombay Presidency government.

In a princely state, the Indian ruler and the state's officials generally administered revenue, education, justice and local public works. However, the British could influence important matters through treaties, political supervision and the appointment of a Resident or Political Agent. A Resident represented British interests and could interfere in matters affecting British political authority.

These arrangements were not identical in every princely state. The extent of a ruler's freedom depended on the state's political relationship with the British.

FeatureBritish-administered GujaratPrincely Gujarat
Political authorityBritish colonial governmentIndian ruler under British paramountcy
ExamplesAhmedabad, Surat, BharuchBaroda, Bhavnagar, Gondal
Internal administrationColonial officers and departmentsRuler and state departments, subject to British influence
Reform decisionsColonial legislation, provincial administration and local institutionsPrincely government, its officials and local institutions

The Gaekwads and Baroda State

The Gaekwads were a Maratha ruling family. Their political position in Gujarat developed during the decline of Mughal authority and the expansion of Maratha power in the 18th century. Pilaji Gaekwad played an important role in establishing Maratha influence around Baroda. Gaekwad rule became firmly associated with Baroda from the 1730s.

By the 19th century, Baroda was a major princely state within the British imperial system. Its territory was not one continuous geographical block. It consisted of separated areas, including the Baroda, Kadi, Navsari and Amreli administrative divisions. British districts and territories of other princely states lay between some of these areas.

This geographical arrangement explains why places in different parts of present-day Gujarat could come under Baroda State's administration. For example, an educational measure introduced in Amreli could later be extended to the other divisions of the same princely state.

Why this distinction matters for reforms

The British introduced educational institutions, administrative departments and municipal bodies in their directly governed territories. Princely rulers could introduce different measures within their own states. Consequently, a reform adopted in Baroda did not automatically become law throughout the Bombay Presidency or the other princely states of Gujarat.

Baroda became particularly important because Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III used the state's internal administrative powers to promote schooling, public libraries, social reform, industry and public works. These initiatives demonstrate how an Indian ruler could pursue an active programme of reform while remaining politically subordinate to the British Empire.

Prelims focus

  • The Gaekwads were a Maratha ruling family associated with Baroda.
  • Ahmedabad and Surat were part of British-administered Gujarat; Baroda was a princely state.
  • Baroda State included the Baroda, Kadi, Navsari and Amreli divisions.
  • A British Resident represented British political interests in a princely state.
  • Trap: A reform introduced in Baroda State did not automatically apply to every part of present-day Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, From Trade to Territory, pp. 15–17, 2020–21 reprint; Government of Gujarat, History of Vadodara, NRI Division website, section on Gaekwad rule, accessed 20 November 2026; Meeta Kumar, Literally Different? Compulsory Education in Baroda, 1881–1931, section 2.1, accessed 20 November 2026.]

title: Colonial Gujarat: British-Administered Districts and Princely States

body:
From Gopalrao to Maharaja Sayajirao III

Sayajirao Gaekwad III ruled Baroda from 1875 to 1939. His original name was Gopalrao Gaekwad. Following the removal of Maharaja Malharrao from power, Gopalrao was selected as successor and adopted by Maharani Jamnabai on 27 May 1875. He ascended the throne on 16 June 1875.

Because Sayajirao was still a minor, a Council of Regency administered the state during his early reign. He received training in government and administration under the guidance of Sir T. Madhava Rao, an experienced administrator, and the tutor F. A. H. Elliot. Sayajirao assumed full ruling powers on 28 December 1881.

The year 1875 marks Sayajirao's accession to the throne, while 1881 marks his assumption of full ruling powers. They refer to different events.

The purpose of administrative reform

Sayajirao sought to make the government more systematic and more responsive to public needs. His priorities included education, agriculture, judicial administration, public works and the welfare of disadvantaged communities.

As Baroda consisted of geographically separated divisions, administration required coordination between the capital and officials working in different parts of the state. Clearer departmental responsibility, improved supervision and regular financial procedures helped the government carry out policies beyond Baroda city.

Revenue, budgeting and audit

Revenue administration concerns the assessment and collection of government income, particularly land revenue in an agricultural society. Reform in this field affected both cultivators and the resources available for public services.

The Baroda government introduced more systematic financial administration, including annual budgets and regular audits. A budget sets out proposed government receipts and expenditure. An audit examines financial records to check whether money has been accounted for properly. These procedures helped officials supervise public spending and plan expenditure on education, transport and other services.

Village panchayats and the Dhara Sabha

Sayajirao also supported village-level participation through panchayats and developed the Dhara Sabha, a legislative institution of Baroda State. Panchayats were associated with local concerns, while the Dhara Sabha formed part of the state's institutional arrangements for considering public matters and legislation.

These measures represented attempts to introduce more organised public administration and limited participation. They should not be confused with a modern system of universal adult franchise or a fully sovereign democratic legislature. Ultimate authority remained with the princely government, subject to British paramountcy.

Administrative initiative under British supervision

Sayajirao could direct many internal reforms, but he did not possess the freedom of an independent national government. British Residents and imperial authorities continued to influence the state's political position. Sayajirao sometimes disputed British interference, illustrating the tension between princely autonomy in internal affairs and the superior authority claimed by the British.

This distinction explains both the importance and the limits of his reforms. He could establish institutions and change administrative practices within Baroda, but his decisions did not alter the constitutional relationship between the British Empire and the princely state.

Prelims focus

  • Gopalrao Gaekwad was adopted by Maharani Jamnabai on 27 May 1875.
  • Sayajirao III ascended the Baroda throne on 16 June 1875.
  • He assumed full ruling powers on 28 December 1881.
  • Sir T. Madhava Rao was an important administrative mentor.
  • Annual budgets, audits, panchayats and the Dhara Sabha were associated with administrative reform.
  • Trap: Internal reform powers did not make Baroda independent of British paramountcy.

[Sources: The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Visionary Maharaja of Baroda, sections Biography, Rules and Regulations, and Heritage and Views, accessed 20 November 2026; C. P. Vashishth, Pioneers of Public Library Movement in India: Part-1, sections 1 and 1.1, INFLIBNET e-PG Pathshala, accessed 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, From Trade to Territory, pp. 15–17, 2020–21 reprint.]

title: Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III: Accession, Rule and Administrative Reforms

body:
Why primary education became a major reform

In 19th-century India, access to formal schooling was unequal. Many rural families faced poverty, distance from schools and the need for children to contribute to household or agricultural work. Girls and children from communities subjected to caste discrimination faced additional barriers.

Sayajirao considered education essential for social improvement and effective public administration. His government expanded schools and treated basic literacy as a public responsibility rather than something to be left entirely to the resources of individual families.

What free and compulsory education meant

Free primary education means that the specified schooling is provided without tuition fees. Compulsory primary education means that children covered by the applicable rules are required to attend school, subject to the conditions and exemptions established by those rules.

Free and compulsory education are related but distinct reforms. Removing fees reduces a financial barrier. Requiring attendance seeks to address irregular enrolment and the practice of keeping school-age children away from school. Neither measure alone guarantees that a school is nearby, that every child attends regularly or that every child completes the course.

The Amreli experiment of 1893

The important starting point was Amreli in 1893. The Baroda administration introduced free and compulsory vernacular primary education experimentally in Amreli taluka. The requirement covered boys aged 7-12 and girls aged 7-10 living within 1 mile of a school, unless they were privately taught or had already passed Vernacular Standard IV.

The government expanded the provision of schools alongside this policy. The experience demonstrated that a princely government could attempt compulsory schooling through state administration, rather than relying only on voluntary attendance.

Amreli belonged to Baroda State even though it was geographically separate from Baroda city. Thus, the experiment was a Baroda State measure implemented first in Amreli, not a general law introduced by the British government for the whole Bombay Presidency.

Extension across Baroda State in 1906

In 1906, the Baroda government extended the policy of free and compulsory primary education throughout the princely state. This was a major step in Indian educational history, particularly because comparable comprehensive compulsory primary schooling had not yet been introduced throughout British-administered India.

State-wide application meant that the policy became a general measure of the Baroda government. It did not mean that every village immediately acquired a school or that every eligible child attended without difficulty. Distance, family circumstances, poverty and social prejudice continued to affect implementation.

Vernacular education and girls' schooling

Vernacular education uses the languages spoken by the local population. Gujarati and Marathi were important languages within Baroda's educational system. English was associated particularly with higher levels of study and Anglo-vernacular institutions.

The state expanded schooling for girls as well as boys. This mattered because girls' education was often opposed on the grounds of prevailing social customs and expectations about domestic responsibilities. By supporting girls' schools and requiring attendance for covered age groups, the administration attempted to weaken some of these barriers.

How Baroda differed from British educational policy

British India had already developed a framework of modern educational administration. Wood's Despatch of 1854 encouraged the expansion and organisation of education, and universities were established at Bombay, Calcutta and Madras in 1857. These measures promoted educational institutions but did not establish universal compulsory primary schooling across British India.

Baroda's distinctive contribution was therefore not the introduction of schools or Western-style education for the first time. It was the adoption of an early, state-wide free and compulsory primary education policy by a princely government.

Results and limitations

The policy encouraged expansion of the school system and was followed by substantial improvements in literacy. Historical comparisons show that Baroda made particularly notable educational progress relative to neighbouring British-administered areas by the early 20th century.

However, schooling remained unequal in practice. Differences between boys and girls, between social groups and between settlements with and without convenient school access continued to matter. The achievement was a significant expansion of educational opportunity, not the immediate elimination of illiteracy or social inequality.

Prelims focus

  • 1893: Experimental free and compulsory primary education was introduced in Amreli taluka.
  • 1906: The policy was extended throughout Baroda State.
  • Sayajirao Gaekwad III was the ruler associated with these reforms.
  • Gujarati and Marathi were important vernacular languages in Baroda's educational system.
  • Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854; it was not Baroda's compulsory education law.
  • Trap: The Amreli experiment of 1893 and the state-wide measure of 1906 were successive stages, not competing dates for the same event.

[Sources: J. P. Naik, Compulsory Primary Education in Baroda State: Retrospect and Prospect, 1941, pp. 1–4; Meeta Kumar, Literally Different? Compulsory Education in Baroda, 1881–1931, sections 2.3.1–2.3.3, accessed 20 November 2026; The Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda, Visionary Maharaja of Baroda, section Rules and Regulations, accessed 20 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation, pp. 84–88, 2020–21 reprint.]
